This is Yayue. 11th century BCE to present.
on_screen: Title card: Yayue · China · 11th century BCE to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Yayue was established in the Western Zhou dynasty by the Duke of Zhou under the commission of King Wu.
It evolved through the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, with the Song era marking a major development in orchestra size and theoretical documentation.
The tradition effectively ceased in China after 1949 but saw a revival in Taiwan in the 1960s and mainland China in the 1990s.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Used for ceremonies honoring Heaven, Earth, gods, and ancestors.
It also served as a marker of aristocratic status during diplomatic meetings, hunting expeditions, and military celebrations.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances are strictly divided into civil and military types.
Civil dancers hold a yue flute in the left hand and a feather plume in the right.
Military dancers hold a shield in the left hand and a battleaxe in the right.
Watch for Civil Dance, Military Dance.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The orchestra uses eight material categories: silk (guqin, se), bamboo (dizi, xiao, paixiao, chi), wood (zhu, yu), stone (bianqing), metal (bianzhong, fangxiang), clay (xun), gourd (sheng, yu), and hide (gu).
Listen for the guqin, dizi, xiao, paixiao.
A stately, monophonic sound dominated by the resonance of bronze bells and stone chimes, supported by the breathy tones of bamboo flutes and the plucked strings of zithers.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances occur in imperial courts or Confucian temples.
The setting is highly formal, with musicians arranged in five directions (four compass points and the center) within the courtyard.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Yayue is child of Aak: Korean court music that preserved elements of Song dynasty yayue.
Yayue is sibling of Gagaku: Japanese court music sharing the same name roots but distinct development.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Yayue is deeply tied to Confucian rituals and ancestor worship; outsiders should observe with solemnity and avoid disruptive behavior during ritual performances.
